Quick reference guide to the RCA (phono) connector family
One RCA connector carries one signal; stereo audio needs a pair, component video needs three
Same physical connector shape is reused across several signal types, distinguished mainly by color coding
White or black: left channel analog audio
Green / Blue / Red trio: component video (Y/Pb/Pr)
Introduced by the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) in the late 1930s/1940s to connect phonograph players to radio receivers, hence "phono connector"
Became the de facto standard for consumer analog audio/video well before any formal single specification existed
Photo: CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Female RCA jack (socket), the receptacle mounted on a device that receives a male RCA plug
Coaxial design: a center pin receptacle carries the signal, surrounded by a barrel that grounds against the plug's outer shell
Almost always panel-mounted — on the back or side of audio/video equipment, rarely found on the end of a cable
Carries a single signal per jack; devices expose one jack per channel/signal (e.g. a stereo pair, or a video + audio trio)
Barrel inner diameter: sized to accept the ~9.5 mm male shell
Orientation: no keying; symmetrical around the barrel
White or black: left channel analog audio
Green / Blue / Red trio: component video (Y/Pb/Pr)
Input/output panels on TVs, AV receivers, amplifiers, and DVD/Blu-ray players
Digital coax (S/PDIF) inputs on receivers and DACs
No single formal specification; the connector is a de facto standard maintained through consumer-electronics manufacturer compatibility
Digital coax use is referenced in IEC 60958
Photo: Evan-Amos, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Male RCA plug, the connector found on the end of an RCA cable
Coaxial design: a center pin carries the signal, surrounded by an outer metal shell that carries ground/shield
Introduced by the Radio Corporation of America in the late 1930s/1940s, originally to connect phonograph players to radio receivers
Carries a single signal per connector — stereo audio, component video, etc. use multiple RCA plugs in parallel
Center pin: thin single pin, diameter varies slightly by manufacturer
Orientation: no keying; the shell simply slides over the mating jack's barrel
White or black: left channel analog audio
Green / Blue / Red trio: component video (Y/Pb/Pr)
Adapters exist to Audio/Connector/Ref/3.5mm TRS for stereo audio (common on portable devices)
Analog stereo audio cables (turntables, amplifiers, TVs, mixers)
Subwoofer/LFE cables in home theater systems
Solid center pin, simple crimp or solder construction
Audiophile variant (e.g. Eichmann) with a hollow center conductor and a separate return-signal pin, intended to reduce contact-related signal degradation
No single formal specification; the connector is a de facto standard maintained through consumer-electronics manufacturer compatibility
Digital coax use is referenced in IEC 60958
